claim: TMEM127 is a transmembrane tumor suppressor implicated in trafficking of endosomal cargos.
source: The adrenal tumor pheochromocytoma (PCC) can be caused by activating mutations of the rearranged during transfection (RET) receptor tyrosine kinase, or inactivation of TMEM127, a transmembrane tumor suppressor implicated in trafficking of endosomal cargos.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about TMEM127.

claim: Loss of TMEM127 causes wildtype RET protein accumulation on the cell surface.
source: Here, we show that loss of TMEM127 causes wildtype RET protein accumulation on the cell surface, where increased receptor density facilitates constitutive ligand-independent activity and downstream signaling, driving cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Increased RET receptor density on the cell surface facilitates constitutive ligand-independent activity and downstream signaling.
source: Here, we show that loss of TMEM127 causes wildtype RET protein accumulation on the cell surface, where increased receptor density facilitates constitutive ligand-independent activity and downstream signaling, driving cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of TMEM127 altered normal cell membrane organization and recruitment and stabilization of membrane protein complexes.
source: Loss of TMEM127 altered normal cell membrane organization and recruitment and stabilization of membrane protein complexes, impaired assembly, and maturation of clathrin-coated pits, and reduced internalization and degradation of cell surface RET.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of TMEM127 impaired assembly and maturation of clathrin-coated pits.
source: Loss of TMEM127 altered normal cell membrane organization and recruitment and stabilization of membrane protein complexes, impaired assembly, and maturation of clathrin-coated pits, and reduced internalization and degradation of cell surface RET.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of TMEM127 reduced internalization and degradation of cell surface RET.
source: Loss of TMEM127 altered normal cell membrane organization and recruitment and stabilization of membrane protein complexes, impaired assembly, and maturation of clathrin-coated pits, and reduced internalization and degradation of cell surface RET.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: TMEM127 depletion promoted surface accumulation of several transmembrane proteins beyond RTKs.
source: In addition to RTKs, TMEM127 depletion also promoted surface accumulation of several other transmembrane proteins, suggesting it may cause global defects in surface protein activity and function.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: TMEM127 depletion may cause global defects in surface protein activity and function.
source: In addition to RTKs, TMEM127 depletion also promoted surface accumulation of several other transmembrane proteins, suggesting it may cause global defects in surface protein activity and function.
evidence: This is suggested as an interpretation of the observed accumulation of multiple transmembrane proteins.

claim: TMEM127 is an important determinant of membrane organization including membrane protein diffusability and protein complex assembly.
source: Together, our data identify TMEM127 as an important determinant of membrane organization including membrane protein diffusability and protein complex assembly and provide a novel paradigm for oncogenesis in PCC where altered membrane dynamics promotes cell surface accumulation and constitutive activity of growth factor receptors to drive aberrant signaling and promote transformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Altered membrane dynamics promotes cell surface accumulation and constitutive activity of growth factor receptors to drive aberrant signaling and promote transformation in PCC.
source: Together, our data identify TMEM127 as an important determinant of membrane organization including membrane protein diffusability and protein complex assembly and provide a novel paradigm for oncogenesis in PCC where altered membrane dynamics promotes cell surface accumulation and constitutive activity of growth factor receptors to drive aberrant signaling and promote transformation.
evidence: This is a novel paradigm proposed based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Internalization from the cell membrane and endosomal trafficking of receptor tyrosine kinases are important regulators of signaling in normal cells.
source: Internalization from the cell membrane and endosomal trafficking of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are important regulators of signaling in normal cells that can frequently be disrupted in cancer.
evidence: This is stated as established background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: RTK internalization and trafficking can frequently be disrupted in cancer.
source: Internalization from the cell membrane and endosomal trafficking of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are important regulators of signaling in normal cells that can frequently be disrupted in cancer.
evidence: This is stated as established background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: RTKs internalized by clathrin-mediated endocytosis transition through successive early and late endosomes for eventual degradation in lysosomes.
source: RTKs internalized by clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) transition through successive early and late endosomes for eventual degradation in lysosomes (Sorkin and Fortian, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: When endocytosis or trafficking is impaired, RTKs may accumulate inappropriately at the cell surface or in aberrant subcellular compartments, contributing to cell transformation and oncogenic growth.
source: In cells where endocytosis or trafficking is impaired, RTKs may accumulate inappropriately at the cell surface or in aberrant subcellular compartments, contributing to cell transformation and oncogenic growth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: RET is an RTK required for the development of the kidneys, nerves, and neuroendocrine cell types.
source: RET (rearranged during transfection) is an RTK required for the development of the kidneys, nerves, and neuroendocrine cell types (Mulligan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Under normal conditions, RET is activated by binding of its GDNF ligands and GPI-linked GFRα coreceptors.
source: Under normal conditions, RET is activated by binding of its glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) ligands and GPI-linked GDNF family receptor α (GFRα) coreceptors, which together recruit RET complexes to lipid rafts, leading to downstream signaling through multiple pathways (Mulligan, 2018; Pierchala et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: GDNF ligands and GFRα coreceptors recruit RET complexes to lipid rafts, leading to downstream signaling through multiple pathways.
source: Under normal conditions, RET is activated by binding of its glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) ligands and GPI-linked GDNF family receptor α (GFRα) coreceptors, which together recruit RET complexes to lipid rafts, leading to downstream signaling through multiple pathways (Mulligan, 2018; Pierchala et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Activated RET at the cell membrane is internalized via CME to early endosomes where signaling persists.
source: Activated RET at the cell membrane is internalized via CME to early endosomes where signaling persists, and subsequently trafficked through the endolysosomal system for downregulation and degradation (Crupi et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: RET is subsequently trafficked through the endolysosomal system for downregulation and degradation.
source: Activated RET at the cell membrane is internalized via CME to early endosomes where signaling persists, and subsequently trafficked through the endolysosomal system for downregulation and degradation (Crupi et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Activating mutations of RET or overexpression of the wildtype protein are established drivers in several cancers.
source: Activating mutations of RET or overexpression of the wildtype (WT) protein are established drivers in several cancers (Mulligan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Constitutively active RET mutants give rise to the inherited cancer syndrome multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), which is characterized by the adrenal tumor pheochromocytoma (PCC).
source: Constitutively active RET mutants give rise to the inherited cancer syndrome multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), which is characterized by the adrenal tumor pheochromocytoma (PCC), while activating mutations or increased RET expression are found in a subset of sporadic PCC (Le Hir et al., 2000; Mulligan, 2018; Takaya et al., 1996a; Takaya et al., 1996b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Activating mutations or increased RET expression are found in a subset of sporadic PCC.
source: Constitutively active RET mutants give rise to the inherited cancer syndrome multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), which is characterized by the adrenal tumor pheochromocytoma (PCC), while activating mutations or increased RET expression are found in a subset of sporadic PCC (Le Hir et al., 2000; Mulligan, 2018; Takaya et al., 1996a; Takaya et al., 1996b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: PCC has been associated with inactivating mutations of TMEM127.
source: PCC has also been associated with inactivating mutations of TMEM127, a multipass integral membrane protein broadly expressed at low levels and localized to the plasma membrane, endosomes, and lysosomes in normal cells (Deng et al., 2018; Qin et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: TMEM127 is a multipass integral membrane protein broadly expressed at low levels and localized to the plasma membrane, endosomes, and lysosomes in normal cells.
source: PCC has also been associated with inactivating mutations of TMEM127, a multipass integral membrane protein broadly expressed at low levels and localized to the plasma membrane, endosomes, and lysosomes in normal cells (Deng et al., 2018; Qin et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: TMEM127 has been suggested to facilitate endosomal transition and cargo trafficking.
source: TMEM127 functions are poorly understood but it has been suggested to facilitate endosomal transition and cargo trafficking and has been shown to modulate endolysosomal function in renal cell carcinomas (Deng et al., 2018; Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: TMEM127 has been shown to modulate endolysosomal function in renal cell carcinomas.
source: TMEM127 functions are poorly understood but it has been suggested to facilitate endosomal transition and cargo trafficking and has been shown to modulate endolysosomal function in renal cell carcinomas (Deng et al., 2018; Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of TMEM127 have been identified in both familial and sporadic PCC.
source: Loss-of-function mutations of TMEM127 have been identified in both familial and sporadic PCC, leading to loss of TMEM127 protein or mislocalization to the cytosol in tumor cells (Neumann et al., 2019; Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of TMEM127 lead to loss of TMEM127 protein or mislocalization to the cytosol in tumor cells.
source: Loss-of-function mutations of TMEM127 have been identified in both familial and sporadic PCC, leading to loss of TMEM127 protein or mislocalization to the cytosol in tumor cells (Neumann et al., 2019; Qin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: RET expression is increased in TMEM127-mutant PCC.
source: Interestingly, our recent data have demonstrated that RET expression is increased in TMEM127-mutant PCC (Guo et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent data and supported by a citation.

claim: The presentation of RET-mutant or TMEM127-deficient PCC are not clinically distinct.
source: The presentation of RET-mutant or TMEM127-deficient PCC are not clinically distinct.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the introduction.

claim: Both RET and TMEM127 have been predicted to confer PCC susceptibility through altered kinase signaling.
source: Both RET and TMEM127 have been predicted to confer PCC susceptibility through altered kinase signaling (Mulligan, 2018; Neumann et al., 2019; Qin et al., 2010), however, their relationship has not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: WT-TMEM127 localized robustly to EEA1-positive endosomes.
source: We showed that WT-TMEM127 localized robustly to EEA1-positive endosomes but that colocalization was significantly reduced for two transmembrane domain TMEM127 mutants (C140Y, S147del), which did not show appreciable localization to EEA1 puncta (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Colocalization of TMEM127 with EEA1 was significantly reduced for two transmembrane domain TMEM127 mutants (C140Y, S147del).
source: We showed that WT-TMEM127 localized robustly to EEA1-positive endosomes but that colocalization was significantly reduced for two transmembrane domain TMEM127 mutants (C140Y, S147del), which did not show appreciable localization to EEA1 puncta (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: TMEM127 mutants C140Y and S147del did not show appreciable localization to EEA1 puncta.
source: We showed that WT-TMEM127 localized robustly to EEA1-positive endosomes but that colocalization was significantly reduced for two transmembrane domain TMEM127 mutants (C140Y, S147del), which did not show appreciable localization to EEA1 puncta (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The total numbers of EEA1 puncta in cells were modestly reduced in the presence of TMEM127-S147del and significantly reduced for TMEM127-C140Y.
source: Interestingly, the total numbers of EEA1 puncta in cells were modestly reduced in the presence of TMEM127-S147del and significantly reduced for TMEM127-C140Y (Figure 1B), suggesting a systemic disruption of endosomal formation or stability in response to loss of TMEM127 function in these cells.
evidence: This is a finding from quantification of immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reduced EEA1 puncta in the presence of TMEM127 mutants suggests a systemic disruption of endosomal formation or stability in response to loss of TMEM127 function.
source: Interestingly, the total numbers of EEA1 puncta in cells were modestly reduced in the presence of TMEM127-S147del and significantly reduced for TMEM127-C140Y (Figure 1B), suggesting a systemic disruption of endosomal formation or stability in response to loss of TMEM127 function in these cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed reduction in EEA1 puncta.

claim: GDNF stimulation promoted colocalization of RET with WT but not mutant TMEM127 in EEA1-positive endosomes.
source: In ARPE-19 cells transiently expressing RET and TMEM127, GDNF stimulation promoted colocalization of RET with WT but not mutant TMEM127 in EEA1-positive endosomes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RET and EEA1 colocalization was reduced but not eliminated in the presence of TMEM127 mutants.
source: RET and EEA1 colocalization was reduced but not eliminated in the presence of TMEM127 mutants, suggesting TMEM127 loss may limit RET localization to early endosome compartments.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: TMEM127 loss may limit RET localization to early endosome compartments.
source: RET and EEA1 colocalization was reduced but not eliminated in the presence of TMEM127 mutants, suggesting TMEM127 loss may limit RET localization to early endosome compartments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed reduction in RET and EEA1 colocalization.

claim: TMEM127-KO SH-SY5Y cells had reduced EEA1-positive endosomes compared to Mock-KO cells.
source: We confirmed that these TMEM127-KO cells had similarly reduced EEA1-positive endosomes to our transient models, described above (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RET protein levels were notably increased in TMEM127-KO compared to control Mock-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed notably increased levels of RET protein in TMEM127-KO compared to control Mock-KO cells (Figure 2A), which was consistent with accumulation of a fully mature glycosylated RET form that is found primarily on the cell surface (Richardson et al., 2006; Richardson et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The increased RET protein in TMEM127-KO cells was consistent with accumulation of a fully mature glycosylated RET form that is found primarily on the cell surface.
source: Interestingly, we observed notably increased levels of RET protein in TMEM127-KO compared to control Mock-KO cells (Figure 2A), which was consistent with accumulation of a fully mature glycosylated RET form that is found primarily on the cell surface (Richardson et al., 2006; Richardson et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 1991).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunoblot data based on established knowledge about RET glycosylation forms, supported by citations.

claim: RET accumulation in TMEM127-KO cells was not due to changes in RET gene transcription.
source: This accumulation was not due to changes in RET gene transcription, since TMEM127-KO cells had significantly less RET mRNA in qRT-PCR assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a possible feedback loop modulating RET transcription.
evidence: This is a finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells had significantly less RET mRNA than Mock-KO cells.
source: This accumulation was not due to changes in RET gene transcription, since TMEM127-KO cells had significantly less RET mRNA in qRT-PCR assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a possible feedback loop modulating RET transcription.
evidence: This is a finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A possible feedback loop modulates RET transcription in TMEM127-KO cells.
source: This accumulation was not due to changes in RET gene transcription, since TMEM127-KO cells had significantly less RET mRNA in qRT-PCR assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a possible feedback loop modulating RET transcription.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of reduced RET mRNA despite increased RET protein.

claim: Transient re-expression of WT-TMEM127 in TMEM127-KO cells reduced RET protein levels.
source: Transient re-expression of WT-TMEM127 in these cells reduced RET protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cell surface RET was significantly increased, by approximately fivefold, in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Using a surface protein biotinylation assay (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Reyes-Alvarez et al., 2022) to specifically detect plasma membrane proteins, we showed that cell surface RET was significantly increased, by approximately fivefold, in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO SH-SY5Y cells.
evidence: This is a finding from surface protein biotinylation assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: N-cadherin and transferrin receptor-1 proteins accumulated on the plasma membrane in HEK293 cells depleted for TMEM127.
source: We also saw similar plasma membrane accumulation of endogenous N-cadherin and transferrin receptor-1 proteins in HEK293 cells depleted for TMEM127, and reintroduction of flag-tagged TMEM127 significantly reduced membrane localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from surface protein biotinylation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Reintroduction of flag-tagged TMEM127 significantly reduced membrane localization of N-cadherin and transferrin receptor-1 in TMEM127-depleted HEK293 cells.
source: We also saw similar plasma membrane accumulation of endogenous N-cadherin and transferrin receptor-1 proteins in HEK293 cells depleted for TMEM127, and reintroduction of flag-tagged TMEM127 significantly reduced membrane localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from surface protein biotinylation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The accumulation of RET on the cell surface and reduced RET in early endosomes suggested that TMEM127 loss might disrupt RET internalization.
source: Taken together, the accumulation of RET on the cell surface and reduced RET in early endosomes suggested that TMEM127 loss might disrupt RET internalization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed accumulation of RET on the cell surface and reduced RET in early endosomes.

claim: Minimal RET internalization was detected by 5 min of GDNF treatment in Mock-KO cells.
source: Consistent with our previous studies (Crupi et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2012), minimal RET internalization was detected by 5 min of GDNF treatment in Mock-KO cells and increased over time, with significantly greater internalization detected by 30 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from biotinylation internalization assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RET internalization increased over time in Mock-KO cells, with significantly greater internalization detected by 30 min of GDNF treatment.
source: Consistent with our previous studies (Crupi et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2012), minimal RET internalization was detected by 5 min of GDNF treatment in Mock-KO cells and increased over time, with significantly greater internalization detected by 30 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from biotinylation internalization assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In TMEM127-KO cells, RET internalization was similar at all timepoints and did not increase over time with longer GDNF treatments.
source: In TMEM127-KO cells, RET internalization was similar at all timepoints and did not increase over time with longer GDNF treatments, with significantly less internalization observed after 30 min compared to Mock-KO controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from biotinylation internalization assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Significantly less RET internalization was observed after 30 min of GDNF treatment in TMEM127-KO cells compared to Mock-KO controls.
source: In TMEM127-KO cells, RET internalization was similar at all timepoints and did not increase over time with longer GDNF treatments, with significantly less internalization observed after 30 min compared to Mock-KO controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from biotinylation internalization assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Recycling of internalized RET to the cell surface was reduced in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO cells.
source: Recycling of internalized RET to the cell surface in biotinylation assays was also reduced in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO cells with a smaller proportion of the internalized RET being returned to the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting RET surface accumulation was not due to enhanced recycling.
evidence: This is a finding from biotinylation recycling assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: RET surface accumulation in TMEM127-KO cells was not due to enhanced recycling.
source: Recycling of internalized RET to the cell surface in biotinylation assays was also reduced in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO cells with a smaller proportion of the internalized RET being returned to the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting RET surface accumulation was not due to enhanced recycling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed reduction in RET recycling.

claim: RET internalization into TMEM127-KO cells is not GDNF responsive and remains at a low constitutive rate despite high levels of RET protein accumulating on the cell surface.
source: Our data show that RET internalization into TMEM127-KO cells is not GDNF responsive and remains at a low constitutive rate despite high levels of RET protein accumulating on the cell surface, suggesting that TMEM127 depletion may impair cellular internalization mechanisms, such as CME.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biotinylation internalization assay data.

claim: TMEM127 depletion may impair cellular internalization mechanisms, such as CME.
source: Our data show that RET internalization into TMEM127-KO cells is not GDNF responsive and remains at a low constitutive rate despite high levels of RET protein accumulating on the cell surface, suggesting that TMEM127 depletion may impair cellular internalization mechanisms, such as CME.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed impairment of RET internalization.

claim: In response to ligand, RET is recruited to clathrin clusters assembling on the plasma membrane and internalized into endosomal compartments via clathrin-coated pits.
source: Previous studies have shown that, in response to ligand, RET is recruited to clathrin clusters assembling on the plasma membrane and internalized into endosomal compartments via clathrin-coated pits (CCPs) (Crupi et al., 2020; Crupi et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies and supported by citations.

claim: In Mock-KO cells, GDNF treatment significantly increased colocalization of RET and plasma membrane clathrin structures.
source: In Mock-KO cells, GDNF treatment significantly increased colocalization of RET and plasma membrane clathrin structures (Figure 3A and B) and caused a significant loss of cell surface RET intensity (Figure 3A and B, Figure 4A), suggesting activated RET is being recruited to CCPs and then moving out of the TIRF field as it is internalized into the cell.
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: GDNF treatment caused a significant loss of cell surface RET intensity in Mock-KO cells.
source: In Mock-KO cells, GDNF treatment significantly increased colocalization of RET and plasma membrane clathrin structures (Figure 3A and B) and caused a significant loss of cell surface RET intensity (Figure 3A and B, Figure 4A), suggesting activated RET is being recruited to CCPs and then moving out of the TIRF field as it is internalized into the cell.
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 3A, B, and Figure 4A.

claim: Activated RET is being recruited to CCPs and then moving out of the TIRF field as it is internalized into the cell in Mock-KO cells.
source: In Mock-KO cells, GDNF treatment significantly increased colocalization of RET and plasma membrane clathrin structures (Figure 3A and B) and caused a significant loss of cell surface RET intensity (Figure 3A and B, Figure 4A), suggesting activated RET is being recruited to CCPs and then moving out of the TIRF field as it is internalized into the cell.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increase in RET-clathrin colocalization and loss of cell surface RET intensity.

claim: When normalized for the increased total RET intensity on the cell surface, RET-clathrin colocalization in untreated TMEM127-KO cells was significantly less than in untreated Mock-KO cells.
source: In contrast, when normalized for the increased total RET intensity on the cell surface, RET-clathrin colocalization in untreated TMEM127-KO cells was significantly less than in untreated Mock-KO cells and was not increased by GDNF treatment (Figure 3A and B), suggesting impaired recruitment of RET to cell surface clathrin irrespective of ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: RET-clathrin colocalization in TMEM127-KO cells was not increased by GDNF treatment.
source: In contrast, when normalized for the increased total RET intensity on the cell surface, RET-clathrin colocalization in untreated TMEM127-KO cells was significantly less than in untreated Mock-KO cells and was not increased by GDNF treatment (Figure 3A and B), suggesting impaired recruitment of RET to cell surface clathrin irrespective of ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells have impaired recruitment of RET to cell surface clathrin irrespective of ligand stimulation.
source: In contrast, when normalized for the increased total RET intensity on the cell surface, RET-clathrin colocalization in untreated TMEM127-KO cells was significantly less than in untreated Mock-KO cells and was not increased by GDNF treatment (Figure 3A and B), suggesting impaired recruitment of RET to cell surface clathrin irrespective of ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed lack of increase in RET-clathrin colocalization with GDNF treatment.

claim: The overall intensity of cell surface clathrin puncta was not affected by GDNF treatment but was significantly less in TMEM127-KO cells compared to Mock-KO.
source: The overall intensity of cell surface clathrin puncta was not affected by GDNF treatment but was significantly less in TMEM127-KO cells compared to Mock-KO (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A decrease of clathrin fluorescence intensity in plasma membrane clathrin structures could suggest a decrease in the number of clathrin subunits incorporated per CCP, reflecting a change in clathrin assembly or size.
source: A decrease of clathrin fluorescence intensity in plasma membrane clathrin structures could suggest a decrease in the number of clathrin subunits incorporated per CCP, and thus reflect a change in clathrin assembly or size.
evidence: This is a possible interpretation of the observed decrease in clathrin intensity.

claim: A reduction of clathrin intensity in the TIRF image could indicate an increase in membrane curvature.
source: Alternatively, as TIRF intensity decays exponentially with distance from the coverslip, a reduction of clathrin intensity in the TIRF image could also indicate an increase in membrane curvature.
evidence: This is a possible interpretation of the observed decrease in clathrin intensity based on the properties of TIRF microscopy.

claim: Clathrin fluorescence intensity in epifluorescence images was robustly reduced in clathrin puncta from TMEM127-KO cells, indicating less clathrin and smaller clusters, not more deeply invaginated structures.
source: Clathrin fluorescence intensity in epifluorescence images was robustly reduced in clathrin puncta from TMEM127-KO cells, indicating less clathrin and smaller clusters, not more deeply invaginated structures.
evidence: This is a finding from epifluorescence microscopy experiments that distinguishes between the two possible interpretations of reduced clathrin intensity.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells had a 2D CCP area approximately half of Mock-KO cells (0.008 µm2 vs. 0.016 µm2).
source: Here, we found TMEM127-KO cells had a 2D CCP area approximately half of Mock-KO cells (0.008 µm2 vs. 0.016 µm2; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from diSIM imaging experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: An area of 0.008 µm2 corresponds to a diameter of approximately 90 nm, within the resolving power of the diSIM technique.
source: An area of 0.008 µm2 corresponds to a diameter of approximately 90 nm, within the resolving power of the diSIM technique (Löschberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured CCP area and the known resolving power of diSIM, supported by a citation.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells had a significant decrease in CCPs per cell relative to Mock-KO cells (213 vs 289).
source: Here, we found a significant decrease in CCPs in TMEM127-KO cells relative to Mock-KO cells (213 vs 289).
evidence: This is a finding from diSIM imaging experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: KO of TMEM127 alters the size and quantity of CCPs in a cell.
source: diSIM provides a clear indication that KO of TMEM127 alters the size and quantity of CCPs in a cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the diSIM imaging data.

claim: TMEM127 depletion led to smaller clathrin clusters or CCPs, suggesting that TMEM127 regulates CCP formation, assembly, and/or turnover.
source: Together, our data indicate that TMEM127 depletion led to smaller clathrin clusters or CCPs, suggesting that TMEM127 regulates CCP formation, assembly, and/or turnover.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TIRFM and diSIM imaging data.

claim: There was a significant 1.3-fold increase in intensity of cell surface RET puncta in TMEM127-KO cells relative to Mock-KO cells.
source: In contrast, we observed a significant 1.3-fold increase in intensity of cell surface RET puncta in TMEM127-KO cells relative to Mock-KO cells (Figure 4A), consistent with the cell surface accumulation of RET, but did not observe a decrease in RET puncta in response to GDNF stimulation suggesting impaired internalization.
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells did not show a decrease in RET puncta in response to GDNF stimulation suggesting impaired internalization.
source: In contrast, we observed a significant 1.3-fold increase in intensity of cell surface RET puncta in TMEM127-KO cells relative to Mock-KO cells (Figure 4A), consistent with the cell surface accumulation of RET, but did not observe a decrease in RET puncta in response to GDNF stimulation suggesting impaired internalization.
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: As fewer CCPs are present in TMEM127-KO cells, some of the intense RET puncta are likely not in CCPs but may represent other organization of the receptor at the plasma membrane.
source: As fewer CCPs are present in TMEM127-KO cells, some of these intense RET puncta are likely not in CCPs but may represent other organization of the receptor at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of increased RET puncta intensity and reduced CCPs.

claim: There was a 1.4-fold increase in surface EGFR puncta intensity in TMEM127-KO cells over Mock-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, we saw a similar increase in surface EGFR puncta intensity in TMEM127-KO cells, with a 1.4-fold increase over Mock-KO cells (Figure 4B), demonstrating that protein accumulation at the cell surface is not exclusive to RET in these cells.
evidence: This is a finding from TIRFM experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Protein accumulation at the cell surface is not exclusive to RET in TMEM127-KO cells.

claim: Multiple classes of transmembrane proteins including RTKs (RET, EGFR), cell adhesion molecules (N-cadherin, integrin beta-3), and carrier proteins (transferrin receptor-1) accumulate on the cell membrane in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO cells.
source: We extended this observation using surface biotinylation assays and showed that multiple classes of transmembrane proteins including RTKs (RET, EGFR), cell adhesion molecules (N-cadherin, integrin beta-3), and carrier proteins (transferrin receptor-1) accumulate on the cell membrane in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO cells (Figure 4C and D), suggesting a global effect caused by impaired surface protein internalization.
evidence: This is a finding from surface biotinylation assays shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The accumulation of multiple transmembrane proteins suggests a global effect caused by impaired surface protein internalization.
source: We extended this observation using surface biotinylation assays and showed that multiple classes of transmembrane proteins including RTKs (RET, EGFR), cell adhesion molecules (N-cadherin, integrin beta-3), and carrier proteins (transferrin receptor-1) accumulate on the cell membrane in TMEM127-KO compared to Mock-KO cells (Figure 4C and D), suggesting a global effect caused by impaired surface protein internalization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed accumulation of multiple transmembrane proteins.

claim: Loss of TMEM127 impairs normal membrane processes including formation of clathrin clusters or CCPs and recruitment of cargo, resulting in altered cell membrane composition and accumulation of multiple cell surface proteins.
source: Together, these data suggest that loss of TMEM127 impairs normal membrane processes including formation of clathrin clusters or CCPs and recruitment of cargo, resulting in altered cell membrane composition and accumulation of multiple cell surface proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TIRFM and biotinylation assay data.

claim: Mock-KO cells appeared to have more intense cell surface clathrin puncta that moved actively into and out of the TIRF field at the membrane consistent with rapid formation and maturation of CCPs.
source: Consistent with our fixed-cell images, Mock-KO cells appeared to have more intense cell surface clathrin puncta, and these moved actively into and out of the TIRF field at the membrane consistent with rapid formation and maturation of CCPs.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells had less intense membrane clathrin puncta, which appeared less able to mature as CCPs and internalize into the cell.
source: TMEM127-KO cells had less intense membrane clathrin puncta, which appeared less able to mature as CCPs and internalize into the cell, moving out of the TIRF field.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: CCPs undergo a multistage initiation, stabilization, and maturation process.
source: CCPs undergo a multistage initiation, stabilization, and maturation process (Mettlen et al., 2018; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Clathrin assemblies must reach a minimum threshold for nucleation of CCPs to initiate.
source: Clathrin assemblies must reach a minimum threshold for nucleation of CCPs to initiate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CCP formation.

claim: Clathrin assemblies can result in either small short-lived (<15 s) abortive CCPs that spontaneously disassemble without cargo uptake, or longer lived productive CCPs that effectively recruit cargo for internalization and delivery to the endolysosomal system.
source: These assemblies can result in either small short-lived (<15 s) abortive CCPs that spontaneously disassemble without cargo uptake, or longer lived productive CCPs that effectively recruit cargo for internalization and delivery to the endolysosomal system (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018; Mettlen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells have significantly increased stochastic assemblies of transient small subthreshold clathrin-labeled structures (sCLS) that are unable to recruit sufficient clathrin to form bona fide CCPs.
source: Here, we show that TMEM127-KO cells have significantly increased stochastic assemblies of transient small subthreshold clathrin-labeled structures (sCLS) that are unable to recruit sufficient clathrin to form bona fide CCPs (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from live-cell TIRF imaging and automated detection experiments shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: As a result of the increase in transient structures, there is a resultant decrease in the initiation of bona fide CCPs in TMEM127-KO cells compared to Mock-KO cells.
source: As a result of this increase in transient structures, we show a resultant decrease in the initiation of bona fide CCPs in TMEM127-KO cells compared to Mock-KO cells (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is a finding from live-cell TIRF imaging and automated detection experiments shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: The CCPs that do form in TMEM127-KO cells are smaller, potentially limiting their ability to recruit cargo, such as RET, leading the cargo proteins to accumulate on the cell surface.
source: Further, as indicated by the reduced clathrin puncta intensity at the membrane and reduced area of CCPs detected by dSIM (Figure 3C and F), the CCPs that do form in TMEM127-KO cells are smaller, potentially limiting their ability to recruit cargo, such as RET, leading the cargo proteins to accumulate on the cell surface (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed smaller CCPs and cargo accumulation.

claim: Although there are relatively fewer CCPs formed in TMEM127-KO cells, a smaller fraction of these had lifespans less than 15 s, suggesting CCPs that are able to overcome early assembly defects due to TMEM127 loss are able to mature to productive CCPs more efficiently.
source: Interestingly, although there are relatively fewer CCPs formed in TMEM127-KO cells (Figure 5D), a smaller fraction of these had lifespans less than 15 s, suggesting CCPs that are able to overcome early assembly defects due to TMEM127 loss are able to mature to productive CCPs more efficiently (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from live-cell TIRF imaging and automated detection experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The overall increase in sCLS and decrease in CCPs suggests that TMEM127 depletion may reduce the potential for clathrin to form or stabilize CCPs capable of internalization and compromise the maturation of productive CCPs.
source: The overall increase in sCLS and decrease in CCPs suggests that TMEM127 depletion may reduce the potential for clathrin to form or stabilize CCPs capable of internalization and compromise the maturation of productive CCPs, thereby leading to impaired internalization of RET and other cell surface proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed changes in sCLS and CCP dynamics.

claim: TMEM127 depletion may compromise the maturation of productive CCPs, thereby leading to impaired internalization of RET and other cell surface proteins.
source: The overall increase in sCLS and decrease in CCPs suggests that TMEM127 depletion may reduce the potential for clathrin to form or stabilize CCPs capable of internalization and compromise the maturation of productive CCPs, thereby leading to impaired internalization of RET and other cell surface proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed changes in sCLS and CCP dynamics.

claim: The defect in cargo recruitment to CCPs and CCP assembly in TMEM127-KO cells could reflect changes specific to cargo engagement within CCPs or broader changes in membrane dynamics, such as protein and lipid mobility.
source: The defect in cargo recruitment to CCPs (Figure 3A and B) and CCP assembly (Figures 3C–G–5A–E) in TMEM127-KO cells could reflect changes specific to cargo engagement within CCPs or broader changes in membrane dynamics, such as protein and lipid mobility.
evidence: This is a possible interpretation of the observed defects in cargo recruitment and CCP assembly.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells exhibited a similar distribution of the population of EGFR in immobile, confined, and mobile cohorts.
source: TMEM127-KO cells exhibited a similar distribution of the population of EGFR in immobile, confined, and mobile cohorts (Figure 5F), suggesting that TMEM127 does not disrupt capture of a minor subset of EGFR within tetraspanin nanodomains that occurs in the absence of ligand (Sugiyama et al., 2023).

claim: TMEM127 does not disrupt capture of a minor subset of EGFR within tetraspanin nanodomains that occurs in the absence of ligand.
source: TMEM127-KO cells exhibited a similar distribution of the population of EGFR in immobile, confined, and mobile cohorts (Figure 5F), suggesting that TMEM127 does not disrupt capture of a minor subset of EGFR within tetraspanin nanodomains that occurs in the absence of ligand (Sugiyama et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed similar distribution of EGFR populations, supported by a citation.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells exhibited an increase in the diffusion coefficient of the confined and mobile fractions of EGFR, in particular the latter.
source: However, consistent with broader disruption of membrane dynamics upon loss of TMEM127, we observed an increase in the diffusion coefficient of the confined and mobile fractions, in particular the latter (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from single-particle tracking experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Loss of TMEM127 may broadly impact membrane dynamics.
source: This predicts that loss of TMEM127 may broadly impact membrane dynamics, suggesting that defects in receptor recruitment to CCPs and perturbations of CCP assembly that may lead to accumulation of membrane proteins at the cell surface in TMEM127-KO cells may result in part from broad alterations in membrane dynamics and/or receptor mobility that impact the formation of CCPs and their recruitment of diverse cargo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increase in EGFR diffusion coefficient.

claim: Defects in receptor recruitment to CCPs and perturbations of CCP assembly that may lead to accumulation of membrane proteins at the cell surface in TMEM127-KO cells may result in part from broad alterations in membrane dynamics and/or receptor mobility that impact the formation of CCPs and their recruitment of diverse cargo.
source: This predicts that loss of TMEM127 may broadly impact membrane dynamics, suggesting that defects in receptor recruitment to CCPs and perturbations of CCP assembly that may lead to accumulation of membrane proteins at the cell surface in TMEM127-KO cells may result in part from broad alterations in membrane dynamics and/or receptor mobility that impact the formation of CCPs and their recruitment of diverse cargo.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed increase in EGFR diffusion coefficient and other membrane dynamics data.

claim: Recruitment of RET to CCPs requires interaction with the clathrin adaptor AP2.
source: Recruitment of RET to CCPs requires interaction with the clathrin adaptor AP2 (Crupi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: GDNF treatment increases RET recruitment as cargo to CCPs in Mock-KO cells.
source: In untreated Mock-KO cells, RET-AP2 interaction was minimal but was significantly increased by GDNF treatment, as indicated by increased PLA puncta (Figure 6A), suggesting RET recruitment as cargo to CCPs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increase in RET-AP2 interaction with GDNF treatment.

claim: Association of RET and AP2 was significantly greater in TMEM127-KO cells, consistent with the higher RET protein levels at the cell membrane.
source: Association of RET and AP2 was significantly greater in TMEM127-KO cells, consistent with the higher RET protein levels at the cell membrane, and was further increased by GDNF treatment, suggesting that the RET-AP2 association was not TMEM127 dependent.
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assay experiments.

claim: RET-AP2 association was further increased by GDNF treatment in TMEM127-KO cells.
source: Association of RET and AP2 was significantly greater in TMEM127-KO cells, consistent with the higher RET protein levels at the cell membrane, and was further increased by GDNF treatment, suggesting that the RET-AP2 association was not TMEM127 dependent.
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assay experiments.

claim: The RET-AP2 association was not TMEM127 dependent.
source: Association of RET and AP2 was significantly greater in TMEM127-KO cells, consistent with the higher RET protein levels at the cell membrane, and was further increased by GDNF treatment, suggesting that the RET-AP2 association was not TMEM127 dependent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed RET-AP2 association in TMEM127-KO cells.

claim: In Mock-KO cells, there was robust association of clathrin and AP2 in untreated cells.
source: We saw robust association of clathrin and AP2 in untreated Mock-KO cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assay experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GDNF treatment significantly reduced clathrin-AP2 association in Mock-KO cells, consistent with maturation of productive CCPs and subsequent uncoating of clathrin-coated vesicles and delivery of cargo to endosomes.
source: GDNF treatment significantly reduced association, consistent with maturation of productive CCPs and subsequent uncoating of clathrin-coated vesicles and delivery of cargo to endosomes.
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assay experiments and an interpretation of the observed reduction in clathrin-AP2 association.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells had significantly greater constitutive association of AP2 and clathrin that was not affected by GDNF.
source: In comparison, TMEM127-KO cells had significantly greater constitutive association of AP2 and clathrin and this was not affected by GDNF.
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assay experiments.

claim: AP2 was not closely associated with TMEM127 under any condition.
source: We did not detect association of AP2 with TMEM127 under any condition using PLA (not shown), suggesting TMEM127 is not closely associated with clathrin-labeled structures.
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assay experiments.

claim: TMEM127 is not closely associated with clathrin-labeled structures.
source: We did not detect association of AP2 with TMEM127 under any condition using PLA (not shown), suggesting TMEM127 is not closely associated with clathrin-labeled structures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of detected AP2-TMEM127 association.

claim: In TMEM127-KO cells, AP2-clathrin complexes accumulate but are unable to efficiently support the formation and/or assembly of CCPs to facilitate internalization of cargo proteins.
source: Together, our data suggest that, in TMEM127-KO cells, AP2-clathrin complexes accumulate but are unable to efficiently support the formation and/or assembly of CCPs to facilitate internalization of cargo proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proximity ligation assay data.

claim: The accumulation of AP2-clathrin complexes in TMEM127-KO cells is consistent with the observation that TMEM127-KO cells have significantly higher sCLS nucleation rates, while exhibiting decreased formation of bona fide CCPs.
source: This is consistent with the observation that TMEM127-KO cells have significantly higher sCLS nucleation rates, while exhibiting decreased formation of bona fide CCPs (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a connection drawn between the proximity ligation assay data and the live-cell TIRF imaging data.

claim: The increased proximity of RET and AP2 in TMEM127-KO cells may reflect increased cell surface levels of RET that may engage with endocytic adaptors, but that these interactions infrequently lead to formation or stabilization of bona fide CCPs.
source: It follows that the increased proximity of RET and AP2 in TMEM127-KO cells may reflect increased cell surface levels of RET that may engage with endocytic adaptors, but that these interactions infrequently lead to formation or stabilization of bona fide CCPs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increased RET-AP2 association in the context of reduced CCP formation.

claim: TMEM127 depletion does not directly affect ability of adaptors to associate with clathrin or cargo but may reflect an integral membrane defect that alters normal membrane protein movement and abilities to assemble or stabilize larger membrane protein complexes.
source: These data suggest that TMEM127 depletion does not directly affect ability of adaptors to associate with clathrin or cargo but may reflect an integral membrane defect that alters normal membrane protein movement and abilities to assemble or stabilize larger membrane protein complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proximity ligation assay data and other membrane dynamics data.

claim: In Mock-KO cells stained for ganglioside GM1, stained lipid microdomains were large and continuous.
source: In Mock-KO cells stained for ganglioside GM1, which selectively partitions into membrane rafts (Sonnino et al., 2007), stained lipid microdomains were large and continuous (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In TMEM127-KO cells, GM1 staining was fragmented and microdomains were significantly smaller.
source: In TMEM127-KO cells, staining was fragmented and microdomains were significantly smaller, suggesting inability to assemble large lipid clusters and raft-associated proteins in the surface membrane.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells have an inability to assemble large lipid clusters and raft-associated proteins in the surface membrane.
source: In TMEM127-KO cells, staining was fragmented and microdomains were significantly smaller, suggesting inability to assemble large lipid clusters and raft-associated proteins in the surface membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed fragmented and smaller lipid microdomains.

claim: TMEM127-depletion alters membrane dynamics, limiting formation of multiple membrane structures.
source: These data suggest that TMEM127-depletion alters membrane dynamics, limiting formation of multiple membrane structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lipid microdomain staining data and other membrane dynamics data.

claim: Internalization of activated RET into the endolysosomal system is required for downregulation of RET signaling and eventual degradation.
source: Internalization of activated RET into the endolysosomal system is required for downregulation of RET signaling and eventual degradation (Crupi et al., 2020; Hyndman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: In GDNF-treated Mock-KO cells, RET was rapidly degraded, with a half-life under 2 hr and less than 9% RET protein remaining after 12 hr.
source: In GDNF-treated Mock-KO cells, RET was rapidly degraded, with a half-life under 2 hr and less than 9% RET protein remaining after 12 hr (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: In Mock-KO cells, TMEM127 had a half-life of approximately 5 hr.
source: In these cells, TMEM127 was shown to have a half-life of approximately 5 hr.
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: In TMEM127-KO cells, RET degradation was significantly slower, with a half-life of approximately 6 hr and over 43% of RET remaining after 12 hr.
source: In contrast, RET degradation was significantly slower in TMEM127-KO cells, with a half-life of approximately 6 hr and over 43% of RET remaining after 12 hr (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Impaired RET internalization due to altered membrane dynamics significantly reduces RET degradation, contributing to RET accumulation on the cell surface.
source: These data suggest that impaired RET internalization due to altered membrane dynamics significantly reduces RET degradation, contributing to RET accumulation on the cell surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cycloheximide chase experiments.

claim: Overexpression or cell surface accumulation can frequently cause constitutive activation of growth factor receptors, conferring ligand insensitivity for modulating the intensity and duration of their downstream signals.
source: Overexpression or cell surface accumulation can frequently cause constitutive activation of growth factor receptors, conferring ligand insensitivity for modulating the intensity and duration of their downstream signals (Du and Lovly, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: In Mock-KO cells, RET and its downstream signaling intermediates AKT, ERK, and the mTOR substrate S6 were minimally phosphorylated in the absence of GDNF.
source: In Mock-KO cells, RET and its downstream signaling intermediates AKT, ERK, and the mTOR substrate S6 were minimally phosphorylated in the absence of GDNF and showed significantly increased phosphorylation over time in response to GDNF treatment (Figure 8A and B), consistent with our previous studies (Crupi et al., 2020; Richardson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: In Mock-KO cells, RET, AKT, ERK, and S6 showed significantly increased phosphorylation over time in response to GDNF treatment.
source: In Mock-KO cells, RET and its downstream signaling intermediates AKT, ERK, and the mTOR substrate S6 were minimally phosphorylated in the absence of GDNF and showed significantly increased phosphorylation over time in response to GDNF treatment (Figure 8A and B), consistent with our previous studies (Crupi et al., 2020; Richardson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: In TMEM127-KO cells, RET, AKT, ERK, and S6 were constitutively phosphorylated.
source: In contrast, RET, AKT, ERK, and S6 were constitutively phosphorylated in TMEM127-KO cells.
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: GDNF enhanced RET phosphorylation after 5 min in TMEM127-KO cells but the effect was not further increased by prolonged treatment times.
source: GDNF enhanced RET phosphorylation after 5 min but, unlike Mock-KO cells, the effect was not further increased by prolonged treatment times.
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Phosphorylation of AKT, ERK, and S6 was not significantly increased by GDNF treatment in TMEM127-KO cells.
source: Phosphorylation of AKT, ERK, and S6 was not significantly increased by GDNF treatment in TMEM127-KO cells (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The constitutive phosphorylation of RET, AKT, ERK, and S6 in TMEM127-KO cells could be blocked by RET inhibition using vandetanib, selpercatinib, and pralsetinib.
source: Further, we showed that the constitutive phosphorylation of RET, AKT, ERK, and S6 in TMEM127-KO cells could be blocked by RET inhibition using the multikinase inhibitor vandetanib, and selective RET inhibitors selpercatinib and pralsetinib (Figure 8C), which are clinically approved for the treatment of RET-associated cancers (Mulligan, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Vandetanib, selpercatinib, and pralsetinib are clinically approved for the treatment of RET-associated cancers.
source: Further, we showed that the constitutive phosphorylation of RET, AKT, ERK, and S6 in TMEM127-KO cells could be blocked by RET inhibition using the multikinase inhibitor vandetanib, and selective RET inhibitors selpercatinib and pralsetinib (Figure 8C), which are clinically approved for the treatment of RET-associated cancers (Mulligan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: GDNF-mediated phosphorylation in Mock-KO cells was blocked by RET inhibition.

claim: Cell surface accumulation of RET can promote constitutive phosphorylation and activation of multiple downstream signaling pathways.
source: Together, our data show that cell surface accumulation of RET can promote constitutive phosphorylation and activation of multiple downstream signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunoblot experiments showing constitutive phosphorylation in TMEM127-KO cells.

claim: Oncogenic activating RET mutations are drivers of proliferation and tumor growth in PCC.
source: Oncogenic activating RET mutations are drivers of proliferation and tumor growth in PCC (Mulligan, 2018; Neumann et al., 2019; Toledo et al., 2017).

claim: GDNF treatment significantly increased proliferation of Mock-KO cells over a 3-day period.

claim: TMEM127-KO cells proliferated significantly faster than Mock-KO cells, irrespective of GDNF treatment.
source: TMEM127-KO cells proliferated significantly faster than Mock-KO cells, irrespective of GDNF treatment (Figure 8D), consistent with increased RET accumulation leading to ligand-independent RET activity and proliferation.

claim: Increased RET accumulation leads to ligand-independent RET activity and proliferation in TMEM127-KO cells.
source: TMEM127-KO cells proliferated significantly faster than Mock-KO cells, irrespective of GDNF treatment (Figure 8D), consistent with increased RET accumulation leading to ligand-independent RET activity and proliferation.

claim: Selpercatinib significantly reduced GDNF-dependent proliferation of Mock-KO cells.
source: Selpercatinib significantly reduced GDNF-dependent proliferation of Mock-KO cells.

source: In TMEM127-KO cells, RET inhibition abrogated the increase in proliferation, seen above, and further significantly reduced viability (~20%) compared to Mock-KO cells (Figure 8E).

claim: Vehicle alone (DMSO) did not affect proliferation under any conditions.

source: Our data demonstrate that proliferation of TMEM127-KO cells was RET-dependent and suggest a previously unrecognized sensitivity of TMEM127-depleted cells to RET inhibition.

claim: TMEM127-depleted cells have a previously unrecognized sensitivity to RET inhibition.
source: Our data demonstrate that proliferation of TMEM127-KO cells was RET-dependent and suggest a previously unrecognized sensitivity of TMEM127-depleted cells to RET inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MTT proliferation assays with RET inhibitors.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

source: Our single-particle tracking studies suggest that mobility of membrane cargo proteins like EGFR is enhanced in TMEM127 KO cells, which may decrease capture of cargo at stochastic clathrin assemblies and limit their progression to successful nucleation and initiation of bona fide CCPs.
